outcome: As of the searches run on 11 Oct 2026, the question is still open in every source read: no in-window paper, claim or announcement settles or moves the bounded-p infinitude question. In-window activity concerns neighbouring questions only (Gafni–Tao, Aug 2025; a Shehu–Uka preprint with an undated 'infinitely many ways' claim), and an AI system (AlphaProof Nexus) attempted Erdős #17 without solving it.
problem_asks: One question: is the set of cluster primes infinite? The statement does not define 'cluster prime'; the definition used in the literature, Wikipedia, erdosproblems.com/17 and the DeepMind Lean file is: an odd prime p (2 excluded by convention) such that every even n with 2 ≤ n ≤ p−3 can be written as q1 − q2 with q1, q2 prime and both q1, q2 ≤ p. Parts: (a) whether there are infinitely many primes p with this property. The statement asks for no bound, no count, no reciprocal sum and no prime-tuple statement; the known counting bounds (1999, 2003) and the finiteness of the reciprocal sum are context, not parts of the question. The condition is bounded in p for each prime, so it is not the unbounded 'every even number is a difference of primes' question.

events.what_happened: Richard Blecksmith, Paul Erdős and J. L. Selfridge introduced cluster primes in 'Cluster Primes', American Mathematical Monthly 106 (1999) 43–48. Per Wikipedia and the Erdős problem page, they showed the number of cluster primes up to x is ≪_A x/(log x)^A for every A > 0 (Wikipedia: for any positive integer m, C(x) < x/ln(x)^m for large x), and that the sum of the reciprocals of the cluster primes is finite. They related the problem to the prime k-tuples conjecture. The question of infinitude is attributed to Erdős (Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, C1). The paper itself was not readable (scanned PDF).
events.revisions: No preprint or earlier public version found; dated to the January 1999 issue (vol. 106, no. 1). The article's exact receipt or preprint date was not established.
events.delivers: An upper bound on the count of cluster primes (≪_A x/(log x)^A for every A > 0) and the finiteness of the sum of reciprocals of cluster primes. Both concern the size or density of the set; neither shows the set is infinite or finite.
events.remains: Whether the set of cluster primes is infinite: the whole of the problem.

checked_by.who: The American Mathematical Monthly (Mathematical Association of America)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for research articles of this kind
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article after editorial review

events.time_since_posted: About 27 years since the January 1999 issue
events.doubts: OEIS A039506 carries a comment by T. D. Noe (21 Jul 2006): 'The Blecksmith paper gives incorrect values of a(n) for n>8'. That concerns the tabulated counts of cluster primes below 10^n, not the asymptotic bound, and no source read disputes the bound. The paper's text itself was not read.
events.direction: Partial. Gives an upper bound on the count and a convergence result for the reciprocal sum. Wikipedia and erdosproblems.com both state the infinitude is not known, and both cite this paper.

events.what_happened: Christian Elsholtz, 'On cluster primes', Acta Arithmetica 109 (2003) 281–284, DOI 10.4064/aa109-3-6. Per the Erdős problem page, Elsholtz improves the count bound to ≪ x·exp(−c(log log x)²) for every c < 1/8. A search summary of the paper instead gives O(x / exp((1/60)(log log x)²)), obtained with Montgomery's large sieve. The paper notes the problem is related to the prime k-tuple conjecture. The paper's text was not read; the impan.pl page gives only the title, volume, pages and DOI.
events.revisions: None found. Exact acceptance or receipt date not established.
events.delivers: A stronger upper bound on the count of cluster primes below x (the exponent constant is reported inconsistently, see doubts). It bounds the count only and does not address whether the set is infinite.
events.remains: Whether the set of cluster primes is infinite: the whole of the problem.

checked_by.who: Acta Arithmetica (Institute of Mathematics, Polish Academy of Sciences)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for analytic and elementary number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article after editorial review

events.doubts: The constant is reported two ways. The Erdős problem page states 'every c < 1/8'; a search summary of the paper states 1/60. Both cannot be the paper's stated theorem as summarised, since 1/60 < 1/8 would make the 'every c < 1/8' claim stronger than the paper's. Unresolved because the paper's text was not read.
events.direction: Partial. Sharpens the count bound; Wikipedia and erdosproblems.com still state the infinitude is not known.

events.what_happened: Ali Shehu and Jetmira Uka, 'On the Additive and Subtractive Representation of Even Numbers from Primes', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202110.0087, not peer-reviewed. Per search summaries of its abstract (the page itself returned HTTP 403), the sieve-based method is claimed to prove (i) every sufficiently large even number is a sum of two primes, and (ii) every even number is a difference of two primes in infinitely many ways. The summaries give v1 submitted 4 Dec 2021 and posted 7 Dec 2021; later versions are reported as posted in Aug 2025 and 13 Jan 2026 (v24). I did not confirm these version dates.
events.revisions: First version posted 7 Dec 2021 (per search summary, unconfirmed). Many later versions; reported dates Aug 2025 and 13 Jan 2026. The version that first contains the 'infinitely many ways' claim is not established, so the first public written date of that claim cannot be pinned down. If v1 already contains it, it predates the window; if it was added later, it falls inside.
events.delivers: Claims that every even number is a difference of two primes in infinitely many ways. That is a neighbouring question (the Maillet / Kronecker / Polignac family), with unbounded primes. On its face it does not give, for infinitely many p, representations of every even n ≤ p−3 using primes ≤ p, so it does not establish the bounded-p infinitude asked here. Whether the method yields the bounded version was not established.
events.remains: The whole problem: the bounded-p infinitude question is not addressed by the claimed statement.
events.time_since_posted: About 4.8 years since the first version (Dec 2021); no published response found
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed. Claims a result on a famous open problem family (Polignac / Maillet-type), with no independent verification or response found in my searches. The full text could not be read (HTTP 403), so the argument was not checked. The erdosproblems.com #17 forum thread (comment 9 Aug 2025) quotes Ribenboim's remark that it has never been proved that every even number is a difference of primes; the thread does not mention this preprint, and I found no link between them.
events.direction: Neighbouring claim, cutting toward the unbounded version of the difference-of-primes statement (which, if true, would be a different result from the bounded-p question as stated). It does not, on its face, answer the question as asked.

events.what_happened: Ayla Gafni and Terence Tao, 'Rough numbers between consecutive primes', arXiv:2508.06463, submitted 8 Aug 2025 (only v1 listed on the arXiv page). Sieve argument shows almost all gaps between consecutive primes contain a natural number whose least prime factor is at least the gap length, 'confirming a prediction of Erdős'; a more precise asymptotic assumes a form of the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture. Neighbouring topic: gaps between consecutive primes, not cluster primes.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page (8 Aug 2025).
events.delivers: Gaps between consecutive primes and rough numbers within them; it does not address representations of even numbers as differences of primes ≤ p, so it does not bear on the cluster-prime question as stated.
events.time_since_posted: About 14 months; I did not search specifically for responses to this paper
events.direction: Neighbouring result. Does not cut toward or against the problem as stated.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository formalises the problem at FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/17.lean. theorem erdos_17: answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | IsClusterPrime p}.Infinite := by sorry, with IsClusterPrime defined by the Erdős wording (every even n ≤ p−3 is q1 − q2 with q1, q2 ≤ p). Declarations erdos_17.variants.upper_BES and erdos_17.variants.upper_Elsholtz (tagged 'research solved') formalise the 1999 and 2003 count bounds; isClusterPrime_97_isLeast_non_cluster is a complete test. The file contains 3 sorry.
events.revisions: Commit date not visible on the page I read. The date of the file's first posting was not established.
events.delivers: A formal statement of the open problem whose truth value is left as a placeholder (answer(sorry)), plus formal statements of the two known count bounds. No new mathematics about infinitude.
events.doubts: The two bound variants are tagged 'research solved' while their proofs carry sorry in this file (3 sorry in total). The repository's own description notes that formal statements can be inaccurate relative to the original conjecture; this file's definition matches the Erdős wording as I read it.
events.direction: Formal statement only; no answer to the question.

events.what_happened: arXiv:2605.22763, 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' (George Tsoukalas and 20 other authors). The paper reports that its most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems it attempted, and proved 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures. The companion repository's attempt list (erdos_problems_attempted.txt, 353 lines) includes erdos_17. The paper's Table 1 (HTML v2, section 3) lists the nine solved problems as 12(i), 12(ii), 125, 138, 152, 741(i), 741(ii), 846 and 26; #17 is not among them. The repository's output folder shows no erdos_17 file, and the direct path erdos_17.lean returned 404.
events.revisions: v1 submitted 21 May 2026; v2 revised 8 Jun 2026.
events.delivers: Nothing established about Erdős #17. It was in the attempt set and, per Table 1, was not among the nine resolved problems. This is an unsuccessful attempt, not a result.
events.doubts: The outcome for #17 is inferred from the nine-problem Table 1 and the missing proof file, not from a stated failure. Only the first 100,000 of about 204,000 characters of the HTML were read; the rest (appendices) was not read.
events.direction: No result on the problem. The attempt did not produce a solution for #17.

summary: Every source read treats the problem as open. erdosproblems.com/17 (last edited 28 Dec 2025; a revision dated 20 Oct 2025 whose change is not described) asks the question and lists no solution, partial result or AI claim; its forum has one comment (Dogmachine, 9 Aug 2025) that is not a claim. Wikipedia's Cluster prime article (last edited 1 Oct 2026) says it is not known whether there are infinitely many cluster primes. The OEIS sequences A038134 (cluster primes) and A038133 (odd primes that are not cluster primes) are the reverse of how erdosproblems.com cites them; the A038134 comment and MathWorld report no progress. The three pre-window or neighbouring papers I opened do not settle the question. Blecksmith–Erdős–Selfridge (1999) and Elsholtz (2003) bound the count of cluster primes, and Elsholtz's constant is reported inconsistently (c < 1/8 on erdosproblems.com, 1/60 in a search summary of the paper). Gafni–Tao (arXiv:2508.06463, 8 Aug 2025) concerns rough numbers between consecutive primes and does not touch this problem. The Shehu–Uka preprint (Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202110.0087, first posted Dec 2021 per a search summary) claims every even number is a difference of two primes in infinitely many ways. That is a neighbouring, unbounded statement, and I could not establish when the claim first appeared, so its date is left null. It is unreviewed and its text was not readable (HTTP 403). On AI: no source I read ties an AI system to a cluster-prime result. AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763) attempted erdos_17 among 353 open problems, but it is not among the nine solved (Table 1) and no proof file exists at the expected path; the paper says its LLM loops are 'based on Gemini 3.1 Pro'. The OpenAI Astra announcement (1 Aug 2026) and the Gemini review of 700 'Open' conjectures (arXiv:2601.22401) name other Erdős problems in the sources I read; neither was shown to include #17, but I did not read OpenAI's primary report and the full Gemini list was not visible. Tao's AI-contributions wiki, as read through WebFetch, has no row for #17, but that read was a summary of a large page and is not conclusive. Name-sharing 'cluster' results (Baker–Pollack 2015 on square-free translates; 'Dense clusters of primes in subsets', arXiv 1405.2593; a Jan 2026 blog's 'prime cluster' notion) are different concepts seen only in snippets. The largest open lead is althofer.de/erdos_cluster_findings.pdf, a PDF titled 'erdos cluster findings' on the homepage of Ingo Althöfer, whose site hosts a 2026 'Math with AI' diary. I could not read the PDF (WebFetch returned compressed binary; a pipeline to extract its text was blocked by a permission check). The diary (March–September 2026) has no cluster-prime entry, so the PDF's content, date and any AI role are unknown. If it claims a result on cluster primes, it is an event I could not record.
competing_reading: One could read the problem as having moved in the window. (1) The Althöfer PDF, if it is a computation or partial result about cluster primes made with an AI system, would be an in-window AI-involved event; I could not read it. (2) The Shehu–Uka preprint, if its 'infinitely many ways' argument also gives the bounded-p representations, would settle the question for an author with no visible review; I found no evidence it does, and I could not read its text. (3) AlphaProof Nexus's attempt on #17, though unsuccessful, is a documented AI attempt, so the problem has an AI-involved attempt even though nothing was produced. Against all of these: the erdosproblems.com page, Wikipedia and the Lean statement all still show the question open after the window.
what_would_settle_it: Extracting text from althofer.de/erdos_cluster_findings.pdf (title, date, claim, any AI-system sentence) and the Althöfer diary entry describing it. The Shehu–Uka version history, to date the 'infinitely many ways' claim and to test whether it extends to the bounded version; the full text is needed, since the preprints.org page returned 403. The Elsholtz paper's stated theorem, to settle the constant. The full AlphaProof Nexus output listing, to confirm #17 has no solution file. The erdosproblems.com #17 history after 20 Oct 2025, to confirm there is no unrecorded status change.

events.credibility_reason: Unreviewed preprint claiming a famous open Polignac/Maillet-type result, many revisions (v24), no engagement found, text unread (HTTP 403).

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether cluster primes are infinite. The 1999 and 2003 papers bound the count from above (and show the reciprocal sum converges), which constrains the set's size without settling infinitude; both are pre-snapshot journal papers, so bound/digested. Close call: an upper bound on the count does not push toward either answer on infinitude, so 'none' was also defensible; 'bound' was chosen as it moves a quantity on the problem, and both are pre-snapshot so the choice does not affect the outcome. Shehu–Uka claims an unbounded difference-of-primes statement, a different question (variant), with an undatable claim. Gafni–Tao concerns rough numbers in prime gaps, a neighbouring problem (variant). The Lean file is a formal statement only (none). AlphaProof Nexus attempted #17 and produced nothing; an unsuccessful attempt carries no mathematics, so scope none and AI role none.
judgement.doubts: The Althöfer PDF 'erdos cluster findings' was never read and could hold an in-window, possibly AI-assisted, result; the record cannot rule this out. Elsholtz's constant (1/8 vs 1/60) is unresolved but irrelevant to the outcome.
